Chemogenetic and optogenetic control of representative physiological processes

Chemogenetic and optogenetic control of representative physiological processes. (a) Subcellular organelle repositioning. CRISPR-GO repositions genomic loci relative to key subnuclear compartments, such as the nuclear periphery, Cajal bodies, and promyelocytic leukemia bodies in a chemically inducible manner. LiMETER enables light-induced ER–plasma membrane contact site formation and manipulation of intermembrane gap distances to regulate the diffusion of membrane proteins at the nanoscale. (b) Remote control over ion channels. COSMO-STIM1ct induces calcium influx in mammalian cells via caffeine-induced dimerization of the cytosolic STIM1 fragment, leading to ORAI1 channel activation. LOCa directly incorporates LOV2 into an engineered ORAI1 mutant (H171D/ P245T) for light-induced channel gating. (c) Inducible programmed cell death. iCasp9 utilizes AP1903-induced dimerization of FKBP12 (F36V) fused with the caspase-9 catalytic domain to activate the apoptosis pathway. The LiPOP1 system employs CRY2-induced MLKL oligomerization and plasma membrane translocation to trigger necroptosis, whereas light-activatable RIPK3 or La-RIPK3 induces lytic cell death by CRY2olig-mediated RIPK3 oligomerization. (d) Conditional genome editing tools. The split-Cas13b/dCas13b system utilizes ABA-induced dimerization for RNA manipulation in an ABA-dependent manner. The CASANOVA system incorporates LOV2 into a specific loop of AcrIIA4, an anti-CRISPR protein, where light irradiation disrupts AcrIIA4 function to initiate gene editing. (e) Tunable CAR-T cell activation for precise immunotherapy. SNIP CAR incorporates the HCV NS3 protease into CAR constructs, ensuring CAR activity only in the presence of US Food and Drug Administration–approved HCV NS3 protease inhibitors. LiCAR utilizes the iLID optical dimerizer in a split-CAR construct to restore immune responses upon light stimulation. In vivo applications are enabled by UCNPs, which convert NIR light into blue emission for activation in deeply buried tissues. (f) Neuromodulation tools. DREADDs rely on designer drugs for selective inhibition or activation of engineered G protein–coupled receptors in neurons. OptoRAF and optoAKT enable precise light-controlled modulation of the Raf-MEK-ERK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways, respectively, to facilitate axon growth and regeneration. Abbreviations: ABA, abscisic acid; AKT, protein kinase B; CAR, chimeric antigen receptor; CASANOVA, CRISPR-Cas9 activity switching via a novel optogenetic variant of AcrIIA4; COSMO-STIM1ct, caffeine-operated synthetic module fused with cytosolic fragment of STIM1; CRISPR, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats; CRISPR-GO, CRISPR-genome organization; CRY2, cryptochrome 2; DREADD, designer receptor exclusively activated by designer drugs; ER, endoplasmic reticulum; ERK, extracellular signal–regulated kinase; FKBP12, FK506-binding protein 12; iCasp9, inducible caspase 9; iLID, improved light-induced dimer; LiCAR, light-switchable CAR; LiMETER, light-inducible membrane-tethered cortical ER; LiPOP, light-inducible necroptosis or pyroptosis; LOCa, light-operated calcium channel; LOV2, light-oxygen-voltage domain 2; MEK, MAPK kinase/ERK kinase; MLKL, mixed lineage kinase domain-like protein; mTOR, mammalian target of rapamycin; NIR, near-infrared; ORAI1, ORAI calcium release–activated calcium modulator 1; PI3K, phosphoinositide-3-kinase; RAF, rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma; SNIP, signal neutralization by an inhibitable protease; UCNP, upconversion nanoplate
